newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's leading parties in high-stakes poker game.
newsitem.headline: Albania's leading parties in high-stakes poker game.

text.p: Albania's two main political parties are locked in a high-stakes poker game that could blow up in their faces and trigger a return to the anarchy that swept the Balkan nation earlier this year.
The issue is the number of seats to be decided by proportional representation in early general elections due at the end of June.

Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino has threatened the resignation of the nine-party interim government if he does not get his way. The next two weeks will show whether President Sali Berisha's Democratic party calls his bluff.
"Everyone is practising brinkmanship," Herbert Grubmayer, the ambassador of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Tirana, told Reuters.

"We hope they will resolve their differences. They have been told by the people who give the money how serious it could be," added Grubmayer, who is coordinating European attempts in Tirana to restore normality in Albania.
He said former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, the OSCE's envoy for Albania, might return to Tirana late next week to try to help bring the parties together.
"If Vranitzky comes he could help to avoid a crisis," said Grubmayer.

The resignation of the government would leave Berisha back where he was in early March, when popular anger over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, in which thousands lost their life savings, sparked widespread rioting across Europe's poorest state.

"Reconciliation and tolerance are essential qualities needed today in Albania. Otherwise, if the political tensions are not resolved democratically it could lead to disastrous violence," a U.N. official said.

Unofficial estimates say that up to a million light weapons, the legacy of isolationist former Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, have been looted from military arsenals and distributed among Albania's 3.4 million population, creating an emormous potential for violence.

An Italian-led eight-nation force of nearly 6,000 troops has been in Albania for two weeks securing the delivery of humanitarian aid, and the high profile Western military presence has helped keep the gunmen off the streets by day.

But at night the capital is alive with the sound of gunfire and the multi-national force has no mandate to disarm Albanians or to act as a police force. It is doubtful they would want to get involved if widespread unrest broke out again.

Berisha's agreement to share power in the National Reconciliation Government and to hold fresh elections calmed passions among Albanians still smarting from the poll last May, described by international observers as seriously flawed.

The Socialists, which was the largest opposition party, pulled out of the election late on polling day, alleging fraud. When the result gave the Democrats 122 seats in the 140-seat parliament, the Socialists refused to take their seats.

The Democrats want to keep the electoral law that won them victory last year, which provides for just 25 seats to be elected by proportional representation, and the rest by simple majority over two rounds.
The Socialists and the other seven parties in the interim government want some 40 seats elected by proportional representation.
Fino has said he will get all the parties together again, probably on Monday, to try to reach a consensus.
If he fails, as the last session did this week, the government will decide by a majority of parties and send a draft to parliament for approval.

If the Democrats fail to accept the majority view in the government, the fear is they will use their huge parliamentary majority to block the legislation. If this happens Fino says it will mean the fall of the government and he will resign.
